questions.q: In clinical biochemistry laboratories, which phase of the total testing process accounts for the highest proportion of all laboratory errors?
options: Pre-analytical phase
Analytical phase
Post-analytical phase
All three phases contribute equally in every laboratory
questions.explain: Studies consistently demonstrate that 60% to 70% of laboratory errors occur in the pre-analytical phase (test ordering, patient preparation, specimen collection, labelling, transport, and centrifugation), whereas automated analytical instrumentation has reduced analytical errors below 10%.

open.q: Which phase of the total clinical laboratory testing cycle accounts for the largest proportion of laboratory errors?

questions.q: Which blood collection tube additive inhibits glycolysis by inhibiting the enzyme enolase, making it the anticoagulant-preservative of choice for accurate plasma glucose estimation?
options: Sodium fluoride with potassium oxalate
Tripotassium EDTA
Trisodium citrate
Lithium heparin
questions.explain: Fluoride ions inhibit the glycolytic enzyme enolase, preventing erythrocytes and leukocytes from consuming glucose in vitro at a rate of 5% to 7% per hour; potassium oxalate chelates calcium to prevent clotting (grey-top tube).

open.q: Name the chemical preservative added to blood collection tubes to inhibit enolase and prevent in vitro glycolysis during plasma glucose measurement.

questions.q: Why must blood collected into a potassium EDTA (lavender-top) tube never be used for routine serum or plasma electrolyte analysis?
options: K-EDTA falsely raises potassium and chelates calcium and magnesium
It precipitates sodium and converts bicarbonate to CO2
It activates alkaline phosphatase and destroys albumin
It causes immediate intravascular haemolysis
questions.explain: K2-EDTA or K3-EDTA introduces exogenous potassium (raising measured K+ above 10 mmol/L) and chelates calcium and magnesium, yielding near-zero Ca2+ and Mg2+ results and inhibiting metalloenzymes like alkaline phosphatase.

open.q: Why does contamination of a chemistry sample with potassium EDTA produce dangerously misleading electrolyte results?
accept: Causes severe hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia by adding potassium and chelating calcium
Falsely elevates potassium and lowers calcium and magnesium

questions.q: Which anticoagulant is preferred for routine plasma electrolyte, urea, and creatinine assays in automated clinical chemistry analyzers because it activates antithrombin III without chelating calcium or adding potassium?
options: Lithium heparin
Sodium citrate
Disodium EDTA
Acid citrate dextrose
questions.explain: Lithium heparin (green-top tube) prevents coagulation by accelerating antithrombin III inactivation of thrombin and Factor Xa without altering sodium, potassium, calcium, or magnesium concentrations.

open.q: Name the anticoagulant commonly used in green-top tubes for emergency plasma electrolyte, urea, and creatinine testing.

questions.q: How does serum differ fundamentally in composition from plasma?
options: Serum lacks fibrinogen and has reduced concentrations of several clotting factors consumed during coagulation
Serum contains intact platelets and erythrocytes suspended in anticoagulant
Serum contains more fibrinogen than plasma because clotting concentrates it
Serum can only be obtained from arterial blood samples centrifuged on ice
questions.explain: Serum is the liquid supernatant separated after whole blood is allowed to clot completely (consuming fibrinogen and prothrombin), whereas plasma is separated from anticoagulated blood and retains fibrinogen.

open.q: What is the key biochemical difference between serum and plasma?
accept: Serum lacks fibrinogen and clotting factors consumed during coagulation
Plasma contains fibrinogen whereas serum does not

questions.q: According to standard venepuncture order-of-draw guidelines to prevent cross-contamination of tube additives, which tube should be drawn immediately after sterile blood culture bottles and before heparin or EDTA tubes?
options: Sodium citrate coagulation tube (light blue top)
Serum tube with clot activator (red or gold top)
Potassium EDTA haematology tube (lavender top)
Sodium fluoride-potassium oxalate glucose tube (grey top)
questions.explain: Standard order of draw places blood cultures first, followed by sodium citrate (light blue), serum/clot-activator tubes (red/gold), heparin (green), EDTA (lavender), and fluoride-oxalate (grey) last so potent chelators (EDTA/oxalate) do not contaminate coagulation or chemistry samples.

open.q: In standard venepuncture order of draw, which anticoagulant tube is collected immediately after blood cultures and before serum or EDTA tubes?

questions.q: In vitro haemolysis of a venous blood sample—such as from forceful aspiration through a narrow-gauge needle or vigorous shaking—falsely elevates the measured serum concentration of which intracellular analytes?
options: Potassium, LDH and AST
Sodium, chloride and bicarbonate
Albumin, prealbumin and retinol-binding protein
TSH and free thyroxine
questions.explain: Erythrocytes contain roughly 20 to 25 times more potassium and over 100 times more LDH and AST than extracellular plasma; red cell lysis releases these analytes into serum and also releases haemoglobin that interferes spectrophotometrically.

open.q: Name three intracellular analytes whose measured serum concentrations rise spuriously when a blood specimen is haemolyzed in vitro.
accept: Potassium, lactate dehydrogenase, and aspartate aminotransferase

questions.q: Prolonged application of a venous tourniquet (>2 minutes) and fist clenching during venepuncture cause venous stasis and water efflux into the interstitium, spuriously increasing the measured concentration of which plasma constituents?
options: Total protein, albumin, calcium, and protein-bound hormones/drugs
Plasma glucose, bicarbonate, and ionized chloride
Arterial pO2 and dissolved carbon dioxide
Urine specific gravity and osmolality
questions.explain: Prolonged venous occlusion elevates capillary hydrostatic pressure, forcing water and small electrolytes out of the vessel while concentrating non-filterable large macromolecules (albumin, globulins, enzymes) and protein-bound substances such as total calcium.

open.q: Why does prolonged tourniquet application during venepuncture spuriously elevate serum total calcium and albumin levels?
accept: Haemoconcentration from water shifting out of vessels concentrates proteins and protein-bound calcium
Venous stasis causes haemoconcentration of plasma proteins

questions.q: A 42-year-old outpatient has a routine serum potassium of 6.8 mmol/L reported on a sample drawn at a peripheral clinic and transported uncentrifuged in a cold box at 4 degrees Celsius for 5 hours. His ECG is completely normal and he is asymptomatic. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Pseudohyperkalaemia from delayed separation and cold-induced pump inhibition
Acute aldosterone deficiency
Diabetic ketoacidosis with normal glucose
Laboratory sodium-calibrator drift
questions.explain: Refrigerating unseparated whole blood inhibits the temperature-sensitive erythrocyte Na+/K+-ATPase pump, allowing intracellular potassium to leak passively into serum before centrifugation (pseudohyperkalaemia).

open.q: What pre-analytical error causes pseudohyperkalaemia when whole blood is refrigerated at 4 degrees Celsius prior to serum separation?
accept: Cold inhibition of red cell Na+/K+-ATPase causing potassium leakage
Potassium leakage from erythrocytes due to cooling before centrifugation

questions.q: Gross lipaemia (turbid, milky serum due to chylomicrons or VLDL) can cause artifactually low serum sodium readings (pseudohyponatraemia) on indirect ion-selective electrode (ISE) analyzers via which physical mechanism?
options: Lipid-related volume displacement reduces plasma water fraction, causing pseudohyponatraemia with indirect ISE
Sodium binds covalently to triglycerides
Chylomicrons stimulate renal sodium loss
Sodium forms insoluble fatty-acid soaps
questions.explain: Normally plasma is ~93% water and 7% solid proteins/lipids; extreme hypertriglyceridaemia or hyperproteinaemia expands the non-aqueous lipid/protein phase, so fixed-volume pre-dilution in indirect ISE assays underestimates sodium concentration in plasma water (whereas direct undiluted ISE gives the true sodium).

open.q: What physical analytical mechanism produces pseudohyponatraemia in severely lipaemic or hyperproteinaemic serum measured by indirect ion-selective electrodes?
accept: Volume displacement by lipids or proteins reducing plasma water fraction

questions.sub: Urine and Other Body Fluid Specimens
questions.q: Why is an early-morning first-void midstream urine specimen preferred for qualitative proteinuria, pregnancy testing, and microscopic sediment examination?
options: It is generally more concentrated after overnight fluid restriction and can improve detection of some analytes
It contains the highest postprandial glucose concentration
It is normally sterile and therefore excludes urinary infection
It remains stable at room temperature for seven days without preservation
questions.explain: Overnight water conservation concentrates solutes, proteins, and hormones (such as hCG) in the first-morning urine, while its lower pH and higher osmolality prevent lysis of red cells, leukocytes, and casts.

open.q: Why is a first-morning urine sample preferred for routine urinalysis and qualitative protein or hCG testing?
accept: It is maximally concentrated and preserves cells and casts
Highest solute concentration after overnight fluid deprivation

questions.sub: Urine and Other Body Fluid Specimens
questions.q: Which chemical preservative is routinely added to a 24-hour urine collection bottle when measuring urinary catecholamines, metanephrines, or vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) to prevent oxidative degradation?
options: Concentrated hydrochloric acid
Sodium hydroxide
Boric acid
Isopropyl alcohol
questions.explain: Catecholamines and their metabolites rapidly oxidize at neutral or alkaline pH; acidifying the 24-hour urine container with hydrochloric acid (pH < 3) stabilizes them throughout collection.

open.q: Which preservative is added to a 24-hour urine collection container to stabilize catecholamines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)?

questions.sub: Urine and Other Body Fluid Specimens
questions.q: When collecting arterial blood for blood gas and pH analysis, why must all air bubbles be expelled immediately from the heparinized syringe and the sample analyzed promptly or placed on ice?
options: Air raises pO2 and lowers pCO2; ongoing cell metabolism consumes O2 and generates acid
Air oxidises haemoglobin and precipitates bicarbonate
Cooling releases calcium from heparin
Room air raises pCO2 to 100 mmHg
questions.explain: Room air has a pO2 of ~150 mmHg and pCO2 near 0 mmHg, so trapped air bubbles shift arterial gas tensions toward atmospheric values; meanwhile, uncooled leukocytes consume O2 and produce CO2 and lactate, lowering pH and pO2.

open.q: What errors occur in arterial blood gas results if air bubbles are left inside the syringe or analysis is delayed at room temperature?
accept: Air bubbles falsely raise pO2 and lower pCO2 while leukocyte metabolism lowers pO2 and pH
Gas equilibration with room air and ongoing cellular consumption of oxygen

questions.sub: Biological Variation and Timing of Collection
questions.q: Which serum analyte exhibits a pronounced diurnal (circadian) rhythm with peak levels between 06:00 and 08:00 AM and a nadir around midnight, necessitating standardized collection times?
options: Cortisol
Creatinine
Sodium
Albumin
questions.explain: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis pulsatility drives peak serum cortisol concentrations in the early morning (around 08:00 AM) and lowest levels late at night (23:00–00:00), a rhythm lost in Cushing syndrome.

open.q: Name a major adrenal steroid hormone that exhibits a pronounced diurnal rhythm peaking around 08:00 AM and reaching its nadir at midnight.

questions.sub: Biological Variation and Timing of Collection
questions.q: Which physiological change occurs when a patient moves from a supine to an upright standing posture for 20 minutes, causing a 10% to 15% increase in measured serum albumin, cholesterol, and total calcium?
options: Standing raises dependent venous hydrostatic pressure and shifts protein-poor fluid into the interstitium
Standing rapidly increases hepatic albumin synthesis
Upright posture immediately suppresses glomerular filtration to concentrate plasma proteins
Standing releases stored albumin from the spleen
questions.explain: Assuming an upright posture increases hydrostatic pressure in dependent lower-extremity capillaries, filtering ~600-700 mL of water into the interstitium and concentrating intravascular macromolecules and protein-bound analytes.

open.q: Why are serum concentrations of albumin, total protein, and total calcium higher in samples drawn from standing outpatients than from recumbent inpatients?
accept: Orthostatic fluid shift into interstitial space causes haemoconcentration
Gravitational increase in lower-limb hydrostatic pressure shifts water out of vessels

questions.q: According to the Beer-Lambert law in spectrophotometry, the absorbance (A) of a monochromatic light beam passing through a clear solution is directly proportional to which two variables?
options: Concentration of the absorbing chromogen and optical path length through the cuvette
Wavelength of incident light and temperature of the tungsten lamp
Viscosity of the solvent and ambient barometric pressure
Incident light intensity and cuvette diameter alone
questions.explain: The Beer-Lambert law states A = epsilon * c * l (and A = -log10 T), meaning absorbance is linearly proportional to analyte concentration (c) and cuvette path length (l) at a given molar absorptivity (epsilon).

open.q: State the two physical variables to which optical absorbance is directly proportional according to the Beer-Lambert law.
accept: Chromogen concentration and optical path length

questions.q: How does turbidimetry differ from nephelometry when measuring immune complexes or particulate suspensions in clinical chemistry?
options: Turbidimetry measures loss of transmitted light; nephelometry measures light scattered away from the incident beam
Turbidimetry measures fluorescence; nephelometry measures electrical conductivity
Turbidimetry uses radioactive tracers; nephelometry uses beta emitters
Turbidimetry measures absorbance by dissolved molecules; nephelometry measures sample pH
questions.explain: Both techniques exploit light scattering by suspended antigen-antibody complexes: turbidimetry measures reduced light transmission along the incident axis using a standard spectrophotometer, while nephelometry detects scattered light off-axis for higher sensitivity at low concentrations.

open.q: What is the optical difference between turbidimetry and nephelometry?
accept: Turbidimetry measures reduction in straight-through transmitted light while nephelometry measures light scattered at an angle
Transmitted light reduction versus off-axis scattered light

questions.q: Which selective membrane composition is used in a standard clinical potentiometric ion-selective electrode (ISE) to measure plasma potassium ions?
options: Valinomycin incorporated into a polyvinyl chloride (PVC) ion-selective membrane
A lithium-lanthanum silicate glass membrane selective for sodium
A silver-silver chloride electrode used to measure chloride by redox reaction
A platinum Clark electrode that measures oxygen tension
questions.explain: The neutral antibiotic ionophore valinomycin has a central cavity specifically sized to coordinate dehydrated K+ ions, imparting high selectivity for potassium over sodium in PVC membrane ISEs (whereas glass membranes measure H+ or Na+).

open.q: Name the neutral ionophore incorporated into PVC ion-selective electrode membranes to selectively bind potassium ions.

questions.q: Why are sandwich (non-competitive) immunoassays generally more sensitive and specific than competitive immunoassays for measuring large polypeptide hormones such as TSH, hCG, and troponin?
options: Capture and signal antibodies bind separate analyte epitopes, producing a signal proportional to concentration
A single antibody binds the analyte without a labelled detection system
Labelled analyte competes with patient analyte, producing an inverse signal
The analyte is separated by gas chromatography before antibody binding
questions.explain: Two-site immunometric (sandwich) assays bind two separate epitopes on large antigens with excess reagent antibodies, achieving lower detection limits, wider linear dynamic ranges, and a positive signal-concentration relationship.

open.q: How does the relationship between measured signal and analyte concentration differ between a sandwich immunoassay and a competitive immunoassay?
accept: Signal is directly proportional to concentration in sandwich assays and inversely proportional in competitive assays

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman with gestational choriocarcinoma has an initial automated serum beta-hCG reported as falsely low (18 IU/L), but after 1:100 dilution of the serum with assay buffer, the corrected beta-hCG reads 480,000 IU/L. Which immunoassay artifact caused the initial falsely low value?
options: High-dose hook effect
Heterophile antibody interference
Carryover contamination
Beer-Lambert inner-filter quenching
questions.explain: In one-step sandwich immunoassays, extremely high antigen concentrations saturate both solid-phase capture antibodies and soluble signal antibodies separately, preventing ternary sandwich formation and producing a paradoxically low signal that rises dramatically upon sample dilution.

open.q: Name the immunoassay artifact in which extreme antigen excess saturates both capture and detection antibodies separately, causing a falsely low result that corrects on dilution.

questions.q: How do analytical accuracy and analytical precision differ in clinical laboratory method evaluation?
options: Accuracy is closeness to the true or accepted value; precision is agreement between repeated measurements
Accuracy describes random scatter; precision describes systematic bias
Accuracy is the same as sensitivity; precision is the same as specificity
Accuracy is measured by coefficient of variation; precision is measured by recovery alone
questions.explain: Accuracy (trueness) reflects how close a measured result is to the accepted reference value (inversely related to systematic error/bias), while precision (reproducibility) describes the closeness of replicate measurements to one another (inversely related to random error/SD).

open.q: Distinguish between analytical accuracy and analytical precision in clinical chemistry.
accept: Accuracy is closeness to the true value while precision is reproducibility among repeated measurements
Trueness to target value versus agreement among replicates

questions.q: How is the analytical coefficient of variation (CV%) calculated from the standard deviation (SD) and mean of repeated quality control measurements?
options: CV% = (SD / Mean) x 100
CV% = (Mean / SD) x 100
CV% = (SD x Mean) / 100
CV% = (True Value - Mean) / SD
questions.explain: Coefficient of variation expresses standard deviation as a percentage of the mean (CV% = [SD / Mean] x 100), providing a dimensionless measure of relative imprecision across different analyte concentrations.

open.q: Write the formula for calculating the analytical coefficient of variation (CV%) from the mean and standard deviation.

questions.q: Which analytical parameter defines the lowest concentration of an analyte that can be reliably distinguished from a blank sample with a stated statistical confidence?
options: Limit of detection
Analytical specificity
Linearity upper limit
Reference interval upper limit
questions.explain: The limit of detection (LoD, or analytical sensitivity) is typically defined as the mean signal of a blank sample plus 3 standard deviations, representing the smallest detectable analyte quantity.

open.q: Name the analytical performance parameter defined as the lowest concentration of an analyte that a laboratory assay can reliably detect over a zero blank.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of daily internal quality control (IQC) using stabilized control sera at normal and abnormal concentrations alongside patient samples?
options: To monitor analytical performance and detect unacceptable changes before patient results are released
To compare the laboratory's performance with all other laboratories each day
To establish the reference interval for every patient tested
To sterilise analyser probes between patient samples
questions.explain: Internal quality control (IQC) provides immediate run-by-run verification that analytical performance remains within acceptable precision and bias limits before validating patient reports.

open.q: What is the primary purpose of running daily internal quality control (IQC) samples in a clinical biochemistry laboratory?
accept: To monitor daily analytical precision and detect errors before releasing patient results
Real-time detection of random and systematic analytical errors

questions.q: On a Levey-Jennings quality control chart, which Westgard multi-rule violation is triggered when a single control measurement exceeds the mean by plus or minus 3 standard deviations (1_3s) and indicates a significant random error?
options: 1_3s rejection rule
1_2s warning rule
10_x trend rule
4_1s shift rule
questions.explain: In Westgard rules, 1_2s (one control outside +/-2 SD) serves only as a warning to inspect further, whereas 1_3s (one control outside +/-3 SD) is a mandatory run-rejection rule sensitive to random error.

open.q: Which Westgard quality control rule is violated when a single QC observation falls outside plus or minus 3 standard deviations from the target mean?

questions.q: On a Levey-Jennings chart, two consecutive control measurements exceeding +2 SD (2_2s) or ten consecutive control values falling on the same side of the mean (10_x) indicate which type of analytical error?
options: Systematic error (shift or trend)
Isolated random pipetting error
Pre-analytical patient misidentification
Post-analytical transcription typo
questions.explain: Multi-point directional rules such as 2_2s, 4_1s, and 10_x detect systematic error—either an abrupt shift (e.g., new reagent lot or recalibration) or a gradual trend (e.g., deteriorating reagent or light source).

open.q: Which category of analytical error is indicated by Westgard rules 2_2s, 4_1s, and 10_x on a Levey-Jennings chart?

questions.q: How does External Quality Assessment (EQA / proficiency testing) complement Internal Quality Control (IQC)?
options: EQA compares laboratory results with peer-group or reference-method targets using externally distributed samples
EQA replaces the need for daily internal quality control
EQA is performed only by bedside nurses using patient samples
EQA measures specimen transport time rather than analytical performance
questions.explain: In EQA programs, participating laboratories analyze identical unknown samples distributed periodically by an external reference organizer, comparing each lab's result against the peer-group or reference-method target to evaluate accuracy (bias).

open.q: What key aspect of laboratory performance does External Quality Assessment (EQA) evaluate that daily Internal Quality Control cannot?
accept: Analytical bias relative to peer laboratories or reference methods

questions.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
questions.q: By international statistical convention (IFCC), how is a health-associated parametric reference interval defined from a Gaussian distribution of results in a well-defined healthy reference population?
options: The central 95% of values in an appropriate reference population
The central 50% interquartile range in every population
The entire range from the lowest to highest observed value
All values within one standard deviation of the mean
questions.explain: A standard 95% reference interval encompasses the central 95% of values from healthy reference individuals (excluding the lowest 2.5% and highest 2.5%), meaning 5% of truly healthy individuals will naturally fall outside the reference limits.

open.q: What percentage of healthy reference individuals falls inside a conventional reference interval, and how is it defined for a Gaussian distribution?

questions.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
questions.q: If a healthy patient undergoes a panel of 20 independent biochemical tests, each defined by a 95% reference interval, what is the approximate probability that at least one test result will fall outside its reference interval purely by chance?
options: Approximately 64%
Exactly 5%
Less than 1%
Exactly 95%
questions.explain: The probability that all 20 independent tests fall within their 95% reference intervals is 0.95^20 = 0.358 (36%), leaving a 1 - 0.358 = 0.642 (64%) probability of at least one false-positive abnormal flag.

open.q: Why does ordering a large multi-analyte biochemical profile in an asymptomatic healthy person frequently yield at least one slightly abnormal flag?
accept: Because each 95% reference interval excludes 5% of healthy people, compounding across multiple independent tests
Statistical probability of false positives increases with multiple tests (1 - 0.95^n)

questions.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
questions.q: Which diagnostic test metric is defined as the proportion of patients with the target disease who correctly test positive (True Positives / [True Positives + False Negatives])?
options: Diagnostic sensitivity
Diagnostic specificity
Positive predictive value
Negative likelihood ratio
questions.explain: Diagnostic sensitivity measures a test's ability to detect disease when present; tests with very high sensitivity produce few false negatives and are ideal for ruling out disease when negative (SnNout).

open.q: Write the formula for diagnostic sensitivity in terms of true positives (TP) and false negatives (FN).
accept: True positives divided by all diseased individuals

questions.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
questions.q: Which diagnostic test metric is defined as the proportion of disease-free individuals who correctly test negative (True Negatives / [True Negatives + False Positives])?
options: Diagnostic specificity
Diagnostic sensitivity
Positive predictive value
Negative predictive value
questions.explain: Diagnostic specificity reflects how well a test avoids false positives in healthy individuals; tests with very high specificity are used to confirm disease when positive (SpPin).

open.q: Write the formula for diagnostic specificity in terms of true negatives (TN) and false positives (FP).
accept: True negatives divided by all non-diseased individuals

questions.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
questions.q: Unlike diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, which remain intrinsic properties of an assay, how does the Positive Predictive Value (PPV) of a test change when applied to a population with a lower disease prevalence?
options: PPV generally falls because false positives make up a larger proportion of positive results
PPV rises because fewer people have the disease
PPV is unchanged because sensitivity and specificity are constant
PPV becomes equal to the negative predictive value
questions.explain: According to Bayes' theorem, PPV = TP / (TP + FP) depends heavily on pre-test disease prevalence; in low-prevalence screening populations, even a test with 99% specificity generates many false positives relative to true cases, lowering PPV.

open.q: How does a decrease in disease prevalence within a tested population affect the positive predictive value (PPV) of a diagnostic test?

questions.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
questions.q: On a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plotting diagnostic sensitivity (y-axis) against 1 minus specificity (x-axis), what does an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 1.0 represent versus an AUC of 0.5?
options: AUC 1.0 indicates perfect discrimination; AUC 0.5 indicates chance-level discrimination
AUC 1.0 indicates chance-level discrimination; AUC 0.5 indicates perfect discrimination
AUC 1.0 means the test has 100% prevalence; AUC 0.5 means 50% prevalence
AUC describes analytical precision rather than diagnostic discrimination
questions.explain: An ROC curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across all cut-off thresholds; an ideal test hugs the top-left corner with AUC = 1.0, whereas a diagonal line with AUC = 0.5 offers zero diagnostic discrimination.

open.q: Which two axes are plotted on a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, and what does an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.5 signify?
accept: Sensitivity versus 1 minus specificity; AUC 0.5 signifies no discrimination (random chance)
True positive rate vs false positive rate; 0.5 means useless test

questions.sub: Post-analytical Phase, Critical Values, and Point-of-Care Testing
questions.q: What is a 'critical value' (panic value) in clinical pathology reporting?
options: A result indicating a potentially life-threatening state that requires urgent clinician notification
Any result just outside the reference interval, regardless of clinical context
A result that exceeds the analyser's reportable range but has no clinical significance
The internal quality-control value used to calibrate the analyser
questions.explain: Critical values (e.g., serum potassium >6.5 or <2.5 mmol/L, plasma glucose <2.2 mmol/L, serum calcium <1.5 mmol/L) require urgent, documented read-back telephone communication directly to the responsible clinician.

open.q: Define a critical (panic) value in clinical laboratory reporting and state the required action when one is detected.
accept: A life-threatening test result requiring immediate direct notification of the clinician
Severely abnormal result needing urgent physician communication

questions.sub: Post-analytical Phase, Critical Values, and Point-of-Care Testing
questions.q: What is the 'delta check' used as an automated post-analytical validation tool in clinical laboratories?
options: Comparing current and previous results from the same patient to flag implausible changes
Comparing serum and urine osmolality to calculate free-water clearance
Checking reagent and room temperatures before each analytical run
Subtracting direct bilirubin from total bilirubin to calculate unconjugated bilirubin
questions.explain: A delta check compares consecutive results from the same patient over a defined time window; an abrupt, physiologically implausible shift (such as a sudden jump in MCV or creatinine within hours) alerts staff to possible mislabelled specimens ('wrong blood in tube').

open.q: How does a laboratory 'delta check' help detect pre-analytical specimen mislabelling or analytical error?
accept: Compares a patient's current result with their prior result to flag implausible rapid changes
Flags unexpected differences between consecutive results on the same patient

questions.sub: Post-analytical Phase, Critical Values, and Point-of-Care Testing
questions.q: Why do capillary whole-blood glucose readings obtained on a bedside point-of-care glucometer occasionally read inaccurately low in a patient with severe septic or hypovolaemic shock?
options: Peripheral vasoconstriction and poor capillary perfusion can make fingertip glucose measurements unreliable
Severe shock converts D-glucose into L-glucose in peripheral tissues
Point-of-care meters measure insulin rather than glucose during shock
Peripheral vasoconstriction causes every capillary glucose meter to report a falsely high value
questions.explain: In hypotensive, vasoconstricted, or oedematous patients, sluggish peripheral capillary blood flow leads to increased local tissue glucose extraction, making fingertip capillary blood glucose significantly lower than central venous or arterial plasma glucose.

open.q: Why should fingertip capillary point-of-care glucometer readings be interpreted cautiously in patients with severe shock and peripheral vasoconstriction?
accept: Poor peripheral perfusion causes falsely low capillary glucose compared with venous or arterial blood
Sluggish capillary flow leads to local glucose depletion and artifactually low readings

questions.q: Under universal/standard biosafety precautions in clinical pathology laboratories, how must all human blood and body fluid specimens be handled?
options: Treat every human blood and body-fluid specimen as potentially infectious
Use gloves only when a specimen carries a visible biohazard label
Recap used needles before placing them in general-waste bins
Mouth-pipette clear serum if no visible blood is present
questions.explain: Standard precautions mandate treating every human blood and body fluid specimen as potentially infectious, wearing appropriate personal protective equipment (gloves, lab coat, eye protection), prohibiting mouth pipetting or needle recapping, and disposing of sharps immediately into puncture-resistant containers.

open.q: State the core principle of universal (standard) precautions when handling patient blood and body fluid specimens in the laboratory.
accept: Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious regardless of known diagnosis
All human specimens must be handled as potentially infectious

questions.q: In clinical toxicology and therapeutic drug monitoring, why is liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) considered the gold-standard confirmatory method over automated immunoassays?
options: LC-MS/MS separates compounds and identifies them using mass-to-charge transitions, reducing antibody cross-reactivity
LC-MS/MS requires no sample preparation, calibration or electricity
LC-MS/MS detects only inorganic electrolytes and cannot identify drugs
LC-MS/MS relies on visual colour changes after adding a reagent
questions.explain: Automated drug screening immunoassays suffer from false positives due to structural cross-reactivity with metabolites or structurally similar drugs; LC-MS/MS combines chromatographic separation with mass-to-charge fragmentation spectra for definitive molecular identification.

open.q: What key analytical advantage makes liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) superior to immunoassays for confirmatory toxicology testing?
accept: High specificity based on chromatographic retention and exact mass-to-charge ratio without antibody cross-reactivity
Eliminates immunoassay cross-reactivity by identifying exact molecular mass
